nameStory: Staurastrum gets its name from the Greek words 'stauros' meaning cross and 'astron' meaning star, perfectly describing these microscopic algae that look like tiny geometric stars or crosses floating in water. The species name 'dilatatum' means 'widened' or 'expanded,' referring to the broad, flattened appearance of this particular star-shaped cell.
description: Staurastrum dilatatum is a single-celled freshwater alga that belongs to a group called desmids - beautiful microscopic organisms that look like living jewels under a magnifying glass or microscope. Each cell is perfectly symmetrical, resembling a flattened star or cross with radiating arms or projections. These tiny organisms are typically green and measure only about 30-50 micrometers across - far too small to see individual cells with the naked eye, though they may contribute to the greenish tint of pond water when present in large numbers.

idTips.label: Star-shaped symmetry
idTips.description: Under magnification, cells appear as perfect crosses or stars with radiating arms, always showing perfect bilateral symmetry like a folded paper snowflake

idTips.label: Flattened appearance
idTips.description: Unlike round algae cells, these appear distinctly flattened and widened, giving them a pressed or expanded look when viewed from the side

idTips.label: Bright green color
idTips.description: Individual cells show a vibrant emerald green color due to their chloroplasts, creating jewel-like appearance under magnification

idTips.label: Clean water indicator
idTips.description: Found only in very clean, unpolluted freshwater - their presence indicates excellent water quality

habitat: Found in clean, unpolluted freshwater environments throughout New England, including pristine mountain ponds, clear lakes, and slow-moving streams with low nutrient levels. These microscopic organisms prefer slightly acidic to neutral water and are often found in boggy areas or woodland pools surrounded by conifers. They're particularly common in the cleaner waters of New Hampshire's White Mountains and Vermont's Green Mountains.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin to grow as water temperatures warm and daylight increases. Best time to find them is in clear, still water after ice melts.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm summer months when conditions are optimal for photosynthesis. Water may show slight greenish tint in areas where they're concentrated.
seasonality.fall: Populations remain active but begin to decline as temperatures cool and daylight decreases. Still readily observable in clean water bodies.
seasonality.winter: Present but much less active under ice cover. Populations survive in dormant state until spring warming begins the cycle again.

funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, a single drop of pond water can contain hundreds of these microscopic 'living stars,' each one a complete organism that's been creating the same perfect geometric patterns for over 400 million years - they were making art before there were eyes to see it!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other star-shaped desmids in the same genus, but the flattened, widened appearance of dilatatum sets it apart from the more narrow-armed or spiny relatives. Remember: 'dilatatum' = dilated or widened, so look for the broader, more expanded star shape.
contextualKnowledge: While called 'algae,' desmids like Staurastrum are actually more closely related to land plants than to seaweeds. They're considered living indicators of ecosystem health - finding them means you've discovered some of New England's cleanest water, as they cannot survive even mild pollution.
compareHints: Staurastrum dilatatum differs from its relatives by its distinctly flattened, widened appearance - while species like S. longispinum have long spines and S. hirsutum appears fuzzy or hairy, dilatatum looks like someone gently pressed a star cookie cutter into green dough. Its arms are broader and less pointed than most other Staurastrum species, giving it a more rounded, expanded look.
